title: Bidirectional BFS in Prague: the shortest route!
description: Watch how Bidirectional BFS shrinks search time by expanding from both start and goal until the frontiers meet. This visualization maps street intersections into a graph and finds the shortest path efficiently.
ig_caption:
🚦 Prague street grid, but smarter: Bidirectional BFS in action! 🧠✨

Instead of running a single BFS wave from the start, Bidirectional BFS launches two BFS searches—one forward from the source node and one backward from the target node—until they intersect. When the frontiers meet, you’ve found the shortest path in an unweighted graph, because BFS explores in increasing distance layers. 📍🔁

On real street maps, each intersection becomes a node and each road segment becomes an edge, forming a graph that can be huge—so meeting-in-the-middle drastically cuts the explored area versus one-direction BFS. 📈🗺️

Want to see your city next? Drop a city + start/end point idea in the comments and follow for more real-map algorithm visualizations! ❤️‍🔥
fb_caption:
Prague (Žižkov) turned into a graph! 🗺️➡️ Think of intersections as nodes and road segments as edges—then we use **graph search** to find the shortest route. 🚦

Bidirectional BFS makes this efficient by growing two BFS frontiers (start↔goal) until they meet, reducing the explored space compared to a single-direction BFS—especially on large real-world maps.
